content:
MARTA KOWAL-BRANDT
QA Automation Engineer | CI/CD and Test Infrastructure
marta.kowalbrandt@example.com | +48 555 303 303 | gitlab.com/mkb-example

PROFESSIONAL SUMMARY
QA automation engineer transitioning into DevOps and platform engineering, with experience owning GitLab CI pipelines and building Kubernetes-based test environments for three product teams. Improved pipeline speed and CI runner costs through profiling and automation. Personal infrastructure projects include Terraform, k3s, GitOps and monitoring.

TECHNICAL SKILLS
CI/CD: GitLab CI, Jenkins, Docker, Docker Compose
Infrastructure and GitOps: Kubernetes (namespace-level experience), Helm, Terraform (personal project), Argo CD, k3s, Ansible (basic)
Monitoring: Prometheus, Grafana, Loki
Cloud and networking: AWS EC2 and S3 (learning basics), Hetzner VPS, Traefik ingress, cert-manager for TLS
Languages and systems: Python, Bash, Java (test code), SQL, Linux, Git, PostgreSQL
Testing: pytest, Playwright, Selenium, Postman

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

QA Automation Engineer, Test Infrastructure | Odrava Health Software | 2021–Present
- Own GitLab CI pipelines for three product teams of approximately 25 developers, covering builds, unit, integration and end-to-end tests, and artifact publishing.
- Reduced average pipeline time from 38 to 14 minutes and monthly CI runner costs by approximately 30% by profiling pipelines, parallelising test jobs, caching dependencies and separating end-to-end tests.
- Built merge-request environments using Docker Compose and later Helm on a shared Kubernetes cluster. GitLab CI deploys the application, PostgreSQL and seeded data; environments are automatically destroyed after merge or 48 hours of inactivity.
- Write Helm charts with namespace-level access; the platform team operates the shared Kubernetes cluster.
- Maintain a pytest and Playwright end-to-end suite of approximately 900 tests. Built Grafana dashboards from CI results to help teams identify flaky tests; the flaky rate fell from 7% to below 1%.
- Wrote Bash and Python tools to seed test data into PostgreSQL, and documented how CI works for internal onboarding.
- Mentored two QA interns in 2023.

QA Engineer | Brightmill Software House | 2019–2021
- Tested web and mobile applications manually and with automation across client projects.
- Introduced a Java and Selenium automated regression suite for the largest client project and configured Jenkins jobs for nightly runs. Previously, a full regression took two people three days.
- Rewrote a small part of the API tests in Python as practice.

Customer Support Specialist, 2nd Line | Brightmill Software House | 2018–2019
- Investigated customer issues using logs and databases and reproduced bugs for developers.

PERSONAL PROJECT

Homelab k3s Cluster with GitOps | 2024–2025
- Built a three-node Raspberry Pi 5 k3s cluster, deploying applications from a Git repository with Argo CD.
- Set up Prometheus, Grafana and Loki for monitoring, Traefik ingress and cert-manager for TLS.
- Provisioned infrastructure for a personal Hetzner VPS using Terraform.

EDUCATION AND CERTIFICATIONS
BEng Computer Engineering | Silesian Lowlands University of Technology | 2018
ISTQB Foundation Level | 2019
Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) | Studying; exam booked for January 2027

LANGUAGES
Polish: Native | English: C1 | German: A2

critique.content_quality_feedback: This is a strong, well-structured and professional CV. It presents a credible QA-to-DevOps transition, uses quantified results effectively, and clearly distinguishes production-like workplace experience from personal projects and learning. The Odrava experience is particularly persuasive: pipeline ownership, ephemeral environments, Kubernetes namespace-level work, measurable performance improvements, and observability are all concrete. The main limitation is not poor writing but scope: the CV demonstrates test infrastructure and platform-adjacent work more strongly than broad cloud infrastructure ownership, systems architecture, or production operations. The transition wording is honest, although it may position the candidate as less experienced than the role's contractor-level expectations.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The document is ATS-friendly: standard section headings, conventional reverse-chronological structure, plain text formatting, and clearly grouped technical keywords. It contains relevant terms including GitLab CI, Kubernetes, Helm, Terraform, AWS, Linux, TLS, monitoring, Python, Java, and PostgreSQL. AI screening probability is moderate to high for junior or transition-level DevOps/platform roles, but lower for this specific contractor role because the CV does not contain Terragrunt or mTLS and has limited evidence of broad AWS operations, systems architecture, security, and production ownership. The phrase "Terraform (personal project)" is appropriately transparent but may reduce keyword strength for a role requiring strong professional Terraform experience.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The CV aligns well with hands-on infrastructure engineering around CI/CD and Kubernetes test environments, analytical problem-solving, observability, Linux, Java-based automation, and clear technical documentation. It also reflects ownership through pipeline responsibility, cost and speed improvements, mentoring, and internal onboarding documentation. The candidate's material does not support strong Terraform and Terragrunt experience, IoT or remote-device integration, mTLS experience, production on-call ownership, or broad cloud operations; these are genuine role gaps rather than document defects. AWS exposure is limited to learning basics and personal use, while the role appears to expect an infrastructure contractor who can design and operate production cloud connectivity from the start. The CV does not currently make the stakeholder-facing aspect of the candidate's merge-request environments sufficiently visible, despite the portfolio supporting QA and product review use.
critique.improvement_instructions:
MINOR, HIGH-VALUE ENHANCEMENTS:
1. In the Professional Summary, replace "QA automation engineer transitioning into DevOps and platform engineering" with a more role-aligned but still truthful formulation such as: "QA automation engineer moving into DevOps and platform engineering, with hands-on ownership of GitLab CI, ephemeral Kubernetes environments, infrastructure automation and observability." This foregrounds infrastructure engineering without overstating production cloud experience.
2. In the Odrava Health Software experience section, revise the merge-request environment bullet to include the stakeholder outcome supported by the candidate portfolio: "Built merge-request environments using Docker Compose and later Helm on a shared Kubernetes cluster; GitLab CI deploys the application, PostgreSQL and seeded data, allowing QA and product teams to review features before merge. Environments are automatically destroyed after merge or 48 hours of inactivity." This better demonstrates bringing stakeholders along and supporting developer and product workflows.
3. In the Odrava experience section, add a separate truthful bullet immediately after the documentation bullet: "Documented how CI works for internal onboarding; the guide is used by new team members." This makes the communication and knowledge-sharing impact more explicit.
4. In the Personal Project section, expand the Terraform bullet to: "Provisioned infrastructure for a personal Hetzner VPS using Terraform; used Ansible (basic) for configuration." This uses the candidate's documented portfolio evidence and improves infrastructure-as-code keyword coverage without implying professional or extensive Terraform experience.
5. In the Technical Skills section, change "AWS EC2 and S3 (learning basics)" to "AWS: EC2 and S3 (learning/basic personal use)" and keep Terraform labelled as "personal project." The revised wording remains ATS-readable while clearly separating learning exposure from professional cloud operations.
6. In the Technical Skills section, change "cert-manager for TLS" to "TLS certificate management: cert-manager". This more directly matches the job ad's SSL/TLS and certificate-management terminology without claiming unsupported mTLS experience.

critique.content_quality_feedback: This is a clear, professional, metrics-led CV with a strong progression from QA automation into CI/CD and test infrastructure. The strongest evidence is highly relevant and concrete: ownership of GitLab CI for three teams, pipeline time reduced from 38 to 14 minutes, approximately 30% lower runner costs, ephemeral Kubernetes environments, and flaky-test reduction from 7% to below 1%. The personal k3s/Terraform project also supports the DevOps transition. The main content weakness is that the target role is substantially broader and more senior than the candidate's current evidence: the CV demonstrates test infrastructure and platform-adjacent work, but not production cloud ownership, systems architecture leadership, or enterprise security/network design. There is also one duplicated bullet under Odrava Health. The CKA status is correctly and transparently presented as in progress rather than completed.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The CV uses standard section headings, plain text formatting, recognizable technology names, measurable achievements, and a parsing-friendly chronological structure. Relevant ATS terms such as GitLab CI, Kubernetes, Helm, Terraform, AWS, Linux, TLS, Prometheus, Grafana, Python, and Java are present. AI screening probability is moderate: the document will likely match CI/CD, Kubernetes, test infrastructure, and junior-to-mid DevOps searches, but it may rank lower for this specific role because Terragrunt, mTLS, systems architecture, security, stakeholder leadership, cloud operations, and remote-device/IoT terminology are absent or insufficiently evidenced. These are primarily genuine experience gaps rather than keyword omissions. The skills section appropriately qualifies Terraform, AWS, and Kubernetes rather than overstating proficiency.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The document aligns well with hands-on CI/CD, Kubernetes-based environment automation, observability, Linux, technical documentation, analytical improvement, and limited AWS/Terraform exposure. It also supports aspects of Corvale's ownership-oriented and collaborative culture through pipeline ownership, mentoring, onboarding documentation, and environments used by QA and product teams. However, the role asks for a contractor who can help shape fleet-connectivity infrastructure from the start and take it to production. The candidate's material does not demonstrate strong Terraform and Terragrunt, production cloud operations, system architecture ownership, mTLS, practical security engineering, IoT or remote-device integration, backend/full-stack development, or virtual-machine experience. The CV should not imply those capabilities. AWS is present only at basic personal-learning level, and Java is limited to test code rather than JVM backend development.
critique.improvement_instructions:
CRITICAL:
1. In the Professional Experience section under “QA Automation Engineer, Test Infrastructure | Odrava Health Software,” delete the repeated bullet “Documented how CI works for internal onboarding; the guide is used by new team members.” Keep the earlier, more complete version only: “Wrote Bash and Python tools to seed test data into PostgreSQL, and documented how CI works for internal onboarding.”
2. In the Professional Summary, make the level and scope of the transition more precise so the document does not imply production cloud/platform ownership. For example, change the opening to: “QA automation engineer transitioning into DevOps and platform engineering, with hands-on experience owning GitLab CI, building ephemeral Kubernetes test environments, automating test infrastructure, and creating observability for CI results.” Retain the Terraform, k3s, GitOps, and monitoring reference as personal-project experience.
3. In the Technical Skills section, retain the existing qualifiers for Terraform, AWS, and Kubernetes and ensure they remain attached to the relevant items. Do not describe Terraform as “strong,” AWS as production experience, or Kubernetes as cluster-operator experience, because the candidate’s information supports only personal Terraform/AWS use and namespace-level Kubernetes access.

MINOR, HIGH-VALUE ENHANCEMENTS:
4. In the Professional Experience section under Odrava Health, revise the merge-request environment bullet to foreground the job-relevant infrastructure terms without overstating scope: “Built ephemeral Kubernetes environments for each merge request using Helm and GitLab CI, deploying the application, PostgreSQL, and seeded data to namespaces on a shared cluster; environments were automatically destroyed after merge or 48 hours of inactivity.” This is more directly searchable for Kubernetes deployment automation, infrastructure lifecycle, PostgreSQL, and CI/CD.
5. In the same Odrava section, combine the pipeline ownership and improvement evidence into a more infrastructure-focused presentation by retaining the exact scale and metrics: three product teams, approximately 25 developers, 38-to-14-minute reduction, parallelisation, dependency caching, separated end-to-end tests, and approximately 30% lower runner costs. These details are among the strongest evidence for analytical thinking and technical ownership and should remain prominent rather than being diluted by lower-value testing detail.
6. In the Personal Project section, make the infrastructure boundaries explicit while improving ATS relevance. For example, use: “Provisioned a personal Hetzner VPS with Terraform and used basic Ansible configuration; built a three-node Raspberry Pi 5 k3s cluster with Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Traefik ingress, and cert-manager for TLS.” This accurately surfaces infrastructure as code, configuration management, GitOps, monitoring, ingress, and TLS without implying enterprise cloud operations.
7. In the Technical Skills section, keep “TLS certificate management: cert-manager” but do not add “mTLS,” network security, Terragrunt, or security engineering terminology unless the candidate later obtains direct experience with those areas. These are gaps in the candidate material, not wording omissions.
